title: Living ashtpadi 9
hook: drop one title and keep the substance

segments.voice: Yesterday, nihkaram: doing deeds, free of them, seeking no reward. Your line was the life, not the title. Did your quiet deed stay quiet? Today, we live ashtpadi nine. Day four hundred seventy-three.

A Sikh family is introduced at a wedding. Harpreet Kaur, her husband Jaswant Singh, their son Arjun Singh, their daughter Simran Kaur, and the grandmother, also a Kaur. Then the woman from another village who runs the langar kitchen: Kaur again. Elsewhere, a surname can tell a stranger your caste, your clan, your rank. These two names are shared on purpose, and they tell the room nothing of the kind. That's ashtpadi nine, carried into everyday life.
screen: `A FAMILY OF SINGHS AND KAURS.` → `SURNAMES THAT TELL YOUR RANK.` → `NAMES THAT DELIBERATELY DON'T.`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi nine took the honored titles of its day, the aparas, the vaishnav, the bhagauti, the pandit, and poured a matching life into each one. Untouched by falsehood. Doing good, not gripped by reward. Teaching your own mind first. Its message, stanza after stanza: the name is nothing without the substance underneath it. Later, Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, making that idea visible. Tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, he gave the initiated men the name Singh, meaning lion, and the women the name Kaur, often explained as princess. The same names for everyone, whatever family or caste they came from. Today some Sikhs use Singh or Kaur in place of a caste surname, and others carry them alongside a family name; there's real variety. But the idea behind the custom is the one Guru Arjan was teaching in Sukhmani. Titles that rank people don't decide who someone is. Living ashtpadi nine, for any of us, can be smaller than a new name. It can be letting go of one title in your own head: the clever one, the responsible one, the one who's always right, the expert. Not the work behind it, just the label. Keep the substance. Drop the badge. Then let people know you by how you live.
screen: `FOUR TITLES, EACH GIVEN A LIFE.` · `THE KHALSA: SINGH AND KAUR.` · `THE SAME NAMES FOR EVERYONE.` · `DROP THE BADGE, KEEP THE WORK.` · then, large: `SUBSTANCE OVER TITLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: do good without a label. First, name to yourself one title you quietly carry: the smart one, the fixer, the good one, the busy one. Hold it for a moment. Then imagine setting it down beside you, like a heavy bag. Breathe. Who are you without it? Probably the same person, just lighter. Today, do one good thing without that label attached: help without being the helper, know something without being the expert. If you pray, you can offer the deed without your name on it. The bell holds the time.
Singh, lion. The name given at the Khalsa's founding, the same for everyone, whatever caste: drop one title, keep the substance.
Your line: substance over title. Today, do one good thing without your usual label on it, and notice who you are without the badge. Day four hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs use the names Singh and Kaur, which tradition links to the founding of the Khalsa, in place of or alongside family surnames, and read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to substance over status.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Singh, lion; the name tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave to initiated Sikh men at the founding of the Khalsa, whatever their caste.

trapdoor: what you thought: Singh and Kaur are just common surnames.
what it means: they're shared names that tell a stranger nothing about caste or rank.

what a scholar hears: the Singh/Kaur naming is associated with the founding of the Khalsa; its consistent use, especially Kaur, became widespread later, and practice varies across families and regions.
